analysis.one_liner: Repeals the entire 2010 health care law and restores the rules from before it.
analysis.headline: The full repeal of the 2010 health care law was referred to eight House committees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase both of the 2010 health care laws — the Affordable Care Act and the budget bill that passed alongside it — and put the law back exactly as it stood before 2010, as if they had never passed [S2][S3]. That would end the Medicaid expansion, the premium tax credits that help people buy insurance, protections for people with preexisting conditions, and the requirement that young adults be allowed to stay on a parent's plan. It would also repeal the taxes that help pay for those programs, which fall mainly on higher-income households, drug makers, and medical device makers.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income households, who would again pay no 3.8% tax on investment income and no extra Medicare tax on high wages; brand-name drug makers and medical device makers, whose annual fees and excise tax would disappear; private student loan lenders, who would regain the federal subsidy system the 2010 budget law ended; and insurers, freed from the law's rules requiring them to cover preexisting conditions and to spend most premium dollars on care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, drug and device makers, lenders

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals both 2010 laws wholesale, restoring every provision of law they changed as if they had never been enacted — which includes eliminating the 3.8% net investment income tax and the additional Medicare tax on high earners that the companion budget law created.
Repealing the Affordable Care Act would eliminate the annual fee on brand-name drug manufacturers and the excise tax on medical devices that the law imposed to finance coverage expansion.
The companion law being repealed ended the old system of federally subsidized private student lenders; repeal would restore that arrangement, with federal payments flowing to lenders again.
Insurers would be released from the law's requirements to accept applicants with preexisting conditions, cap out-of-pocket costs, and spend a set share of premiums on medical care.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people: the millions who gained coverage through the Medicaid expansion or premium subsidies would lose it; people with preexisting conditions would again be denied insurance or charged unaffordable rates; young adults would lose the ability to stay on a parent's plan; and seniors would face higher prescription drug costs with the return of the Medicare coverage gap.
analysis.who_pays_short: Newly insured households and people with preexisting conditions

drawbacks.text: Repeal is written as a clean erasure with no replacement: it restores the pre-2010 legal framework, so every coverage gain the law produced for ordinary households disappears with nothing put in its place [S2][S3].

Because the bill repeals the revenue measures too — the investment income tax, the drug and device fees — the federal government loses the money that financed the coverage expansion, while the tax savings go to higher-income households and affected industries.
Even supporters of changing the health law would acknowledge that a full retroactive repeal creates upheaval for insurers, providers, and states that built programs around the 2010 framework.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are concentrated and the costs are spread: a full repeal would deliver tax and fee relief to high earners, drug makers, device makers, and lenders, while taking coverage and protections away from millions of ordinary people at once. For most readers, the cost side plainly outweighs the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to eight committees, sat at the subcommittee level, and never got a hearing or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King (R-IA) introduced the ObamaCare Repeal Act on January 3, 2013, the first day of the new Congress.
It was referred to eight committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, Rules, and Appropriations.
It was then referred to subcommittees handling health, Indian and Alaska Native affairs, higher education, and labor, and no committee ever took it up further.
It drew only two cosponsors, both Republicans, and never reached the House floor; the Congress ended January 3, 2015, with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on the 2010 health law's coverage expansions and protections came out ahead: because the repeal never advanced, the Medicaid expansion, premium subsidies, and consumer protections stayed in place. The bill's intended beneficiaries — high earners and the drug, device, and lending industries — gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyone covered by the 2010 health law's protections

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full-repeal bill on January 3, 2013.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; subcommittee on health received the bill
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill after referral; it remained at the subcommittee level for the entire Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat supported it; the bill never came to a vote, so no roll-call exists.

industries.note: Repeal would erase the annual fee the 2010 law placed on brand-name manufacturers and the Medicare discounts that narrowed seniors' coverage gap. The fee helped finance coverage ordinary people use.
Repeal would end the excise tax on medical devices that helped pay for the coverage expansion. The industry's gain comes from removing funding for benefits ordinary people receive.

Repeal of the companion budget law would eliminate the 3.8% tax on investment income and the extra Medicare tax on high wages, a direct tax cut for the wealthiest taxpayers paid for by ending coverage subsidies.
The 2010 budget law ended federal subsidies to private lenders and redirected savings to Pell Grants; repeal would restore the subsidized lender system.

Repeal frees insurers from guaranteed-issue, out-of-pocket caps, and medical loss ratio rules, but takes away the subsidies and mandate that brought them millions of paying customers. Consumers would lose the rules that guarantee they can buy coverage at all.
